priors.rationale: Companies that report above expectations have historically kept drifting in the same direction for weeks afterwards - the post-earnings announcement drift. The announcement day itself typically moves the price 2% to 6%; the drift that follows is the smaller part, and it is the only part a next-day entry can reach.
priors.source_note: Ball & Brown 1968 (JAR); Bernard & Thomas 1989 (JAR): drift persists for roughly 60 trading days after the report

priors.rationale: Companies that report below expectations have historically kept drifting lower for weeks afterwards - the negative side of post-earnings announcement drift. The announcement day itself typically moves the price 2% to 6%; what a next-day entry can reach is the slower continuation.
priors.source_note: Ball & Brown 1968 (JAR); Bernard & Thomas 1989 (JAR): drift persists for roughly 60 trading days after the report

priors.rationale: Management forecast revisions move prices because managers know more about the coming quarter than analysts do. An upward revision has historically been worth 2% to 5% on the day, followed by a smaller continuation over the next week as estimates catch up.
priors.source_note: Skinner 1994 (JAR); Anilowski, Feng & Skinner 2007 (JAE): management guidance is among the strongest single disclosures

priors.rationale: Downward forecast revisions are historically punished harder than upward ones are rewarded, typically 3% to 8% on the day, with analyst downgrades trailing over the following week and extending the move.
priors.source_note: Skinner 1994 (JAR): asymmetric reaction to bad news disclosures; Anilowski, Feng & Skinner 2007 (JAE)

priors.rationale: Withdrawing guidance entirely is a stronger admission than cutting it: management is saying it no longer stands behind any number. Historically this has been worth 4% to 10% on the day, with continued weakness while the uncertainty is unresolved.
priors.source_note: Skinner 1994 (JAR); withdrawal clusters in the tail of the bad-news disclosure distribution

priors.rationale: Announced takeover targets have historically jumped 16% to 24% on the day of the announcement, and almost all of that is priced before the next open. What remains afterwards is the narrower spread between the trading price and the offer, which closes only if the deal actually completes.
priors.source_note: Andrade, Mitchell & Stafford 2001 (JEP): target CAR +16-24%, acquirer roughly 0 to -1%

priors.rationale: Acquirers have historically earned roughly zero to slightly negative abnormal returns around a deal announcement - the market prices integration risk and the possibility of overpaying. The effect sits close to the noise floor, which is why this leg carries lower confidence than the target leg.
priors.source_note: Andrade, Mitchell & Stafford 2001 (JEP): acquirer CAR roughly 0 to -1%; Moeller, Schlingemann & Stulz 2005 (JF)

priors.rationale: Enforcement actions cost listed companies far more than the fine itself: the reputational loss borne through lost business and higher contracting costs has historically been several times the cash penalty, and it is absorbed over days rather than instantly.
priors.source_note: Karpoff, Lee & Martin 2008 (JFQA): reputational penalty is roughly 7.5x the legal penalty for financial misrepresentation

priors.rationale: Enforcement actions hit digital assets harder than listed equities because access itself is at stake: venues restrict pairs, market makers step back, and liquidity thins for days after the filing rather than repricing all at once.
priors.source_note: Karpoff, Lee & Martin 2008 (JFQA) for the reputational channel; crypto enforcement episodes show larger and slower drawdowns

priors.rationale: Removing a regulatory overhang - an approval, a dismissal, a closed investigation - releases the discount the market applied while the outcome was uncertain. The release is partly immediate and partly spread over the following days as the constraint on the business is re-underwritten.
priors.source_note: Karpoff, Lee & Martin 2008 (JFQA), read in reverse: resolution recovers part of the reputational discount

priors.rationale: Favorable regulatory outcomes matter more for digital assets because they widen access: venues relist, custodians re-enable transfers, and allocators who were blocked can participate. That widening happens over days, not in a single print.
priors.source_note: Crypto regulatory-resolution episodes; mechanism mirrors the access channel documented for exchange listings (Messari 2021)

priors.rationale: Tokens newly listed on a major venue have historically shown a large announcement pop of 10% to 30% followed by several days of smaller continued drift as access widens to that venue's users and market makers.
priors.source_note: Messari 2021 'Coinbase effect'; Binance-listing event studies report double-digit announcement returns with multi-day continuation

priors.rationale: Index inclusion produces a mechanical demand shock from funds that track the index, but the effect has shrunk as the trade became widely anticipated. What is left after the announcement day sits close to the noise floor.
priors.source_note: Shleifer 1986 (JF) documented the original inclusion effect; later work finds it largely arbitraged away

priors.rationale: Removal from a major venue withdraws exactly the access that a listing granted: liquidity concentrates on thinner venues and holders exit ahead of the removal date, so weakness continues for days after the notice rather than ending with it.
priors.source_note: Mirror image of the documented listing effect (Messari 2021); exchange delisting notices show sustained outflows

priors.rationale: Index deletion forces tracking funds to unwind and removes a stable holder base. The mechanical part lands on the rebalance, but the loss of that holder base continues to weigh in the days around it.
priors.source_note: Shleifer 1986 (JF) and the index-deletion literature: deletions show a larger and slower effect than additions

priors.rationale: Tokens of exploited protocols have historically dropped sharply on the day of disclosure, roughly 10% to 25%, with a smaller continued decline over the following days as the true scale of the loss and the reimbursement plan become clear.
priors.source_note: Ronin/Axie 2022 and comparable bridge exploits: sharp disclosure-day drawdown with multi-day continuation

priors.rationale: Data breaches at listed companies have historically produced a modest and fairly short-lived abnormal decline: the direct costs are insurable and the reputational damage is slower and harder to price than in a protocol exploit.
priors.source_note: Cavusoglu, Mishra & Raghunathan 2004 (IJEC) and later breach event studies: low single-digit abnormal declines
